item.title: The Skin Detector System of the LZ Dark Matter Experiment
item.description: arXiv:2611.00010v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents the design, calibration, and performance of the Skin Detector component of the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) dark matter experiment. The Skin Detector consists of approximately 2 tonnes of liquid xenon instrumented with 131 photomultiplier tubes, surrounding the central time-projection chamber and functions as an active veto system for background rejection. Energy calibration with monoenergetic gamma sources established a position-dependent energy scale and determined prompt and delayed veto thresholds. Radon decays in the Skin can be identified with less than 15~mm spatial resolution, revealing stable convective flow patterns with measured velocities ranging from 2-4 mm/s that persisted throughout extended data-taking periods. The achieved Skin veto threshold meets or exceeds the design goal of 100~keV throughout the Skin volume. The prompt veto efficiency for gamma rays emitted following electron capture in $^{127}$Xe is found to be ($88 \pm 2$)\%, consistent with the simulated value of ($90.4 \pm 0.6$)\%. M-shell EC decays are used to validate the LZ detector sensitivity for low-mass dark matter during the first science run.

item.title: Fabrication and characterization of a micro-boiling meter for heat transfer measurements on a single nucleation site
item.description: arXiv:2611.00057v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate characterization of heat transfer during pool boiling requires sensors capable of resolving rapid transients and highly localized thermal events. Conventional approaches often suffer from limited spatial resolution and slow thermal response due to intermediate material layers. To overcome these limitations and obtain accurate measurements of surface temperature and heat flux during pool boiling studies, we used a boiling meter. Two of these consist of commercially available sensors. To improve the study of vapor bubble dynamics, a third boiling meter was designed, dimensioned, and microfabricated. It was fabricated on a Borofloat 33-silicon composite substrate featuring a suspended Borofloat membrane with a central 200 $\mu$m micropillar and a laser-ablated nucleation site (100 $\mu$m x 115 $\mu$m). Two platinum resistance temperature detectors (Pt-RTDs) were integrated on both sides of the substrate to enable direct, localized, and time-resolved measurements of wall temperature and heat flux during bubble formation. Characterization of the microfabricated boiling meter was carried out in controlled radiative environment and in pool boiling. The microfabricated device exhibited a thermal characteristic time of around 200 ms in radiative tests (more than 30 times shorter under similar operating conditions than the times found with boiling meters composed of commercial sensors), but was able to capture a bubble frequency of 26 Hz, which validates its ability to resolve transient thermal events. Its suspended glass-membrane structure, combined with the direct liquid-RTD interface, provides both high temporal resolution and spatial sensitivity, essential for capturing the short timescales of bubble nucleation, growth, and departure.

item.title: Detectability of an orbital-angular-momentum-based gravitational wave detector
item.description: arXiv:2611.00085v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The orbital angular momentum (OAM) of light provides a new approach to probing gravitational waves (GWs) through transitions between OAM states. Here, we assess the detectability of an OAM-based GW detector by developing a readout scheme and evaluating its noise budget over the frequency range from $1~\mathrm{mHz}$ to $100~\mathrm{Hz}$, including laser-intensity noise, laser-phase noise, mode-impurity noise, and shot noise. For a symmetric superposition OAM state, the GW-induced transition amplitudes satisfy $\alpha_+=-\alpha_-^*$, whereas the noise-induced mode-crosstalk coefficients obey $n_+=n_-^*$. Hence, the GW-induced signal forms a differential-mode contribution, while laser-intensity and mode-impurity noises enter as common-mode contributions, enabling their suppression by the balanced detection. Under a fixed beam-waist constraint, a shorter arm permits a larger paraxial parameter, reducing the equivalent angular-noise strain sensitivity. We adopt an arm length of $L=4\,\mathrm{m}$, $N=160$ round trips, a paraxial parameter of $\gamma=0.1$, a laser power incident on the beam splitter of $P_{\mathrm{BS}}=10\,\mathrm{kW}$, and a wavelength of $\lambda_{\mathrm{opt}}=1064\,\mathrm{nm}$. Using representative noise spectra, we find that, for GWs from an equal-mass binary black hole with source-frame component masses of $M_{\mathrm{src}}=10^{4}\,M_{\odot}$ at redshift $z=1$, balanced detection yields an SNR of $24.7$ for an imbalance parameter of $\epsilon=10^{-3}$ and $239$ for $\epsilon=10^{-5}$, with the sensitivity approaching the shot-noise limit in the latter case. These results highlight the importance of a compact optical configuration and strong common-mode rejection for realizing an OAM-based GW detector.
item.dc:creator: Haorong Wu, Xilong Fan

item.title: SCRAMJet: An Ultra Low Latency JetClass-Scale Transformer for the HL-LHC Level-1 Trigger
item.description: arXiv:2611.00086v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Level-1 Triggers at the LHC classify collisions within a few microseconds on FPGAs, where a network is a fully unrolled circuit whose cost is area rather than time. We present SCRAMJet, a transformer encoder that replaces multi-head attention with a low-rank projection, trains under per-parameter learned fixed-point quantization, and compiles to Verilog with distributed arithmetic optimization. On the ten-class JetClass dataset it reaches $71.4 \pm 0.6\%$ accuracy with 0.157M multiply-accumulates, 6.1 accuracy points above the strongest published resource-constrained model at an eighth of the operations, and meets timing on a Virtex UltraScale+ VU13P at 147 ns using 25.7% of the logic. We also show that resource-aware training silently removes attention channels: one whose learned bit-width reaches zero still carries signal during training but is absent from the compiled circuit, so the loss never sees it go. We call these virtual channels, and a floor on the attention datalane that prevents them is worth 3.1 accuracy points at matched budget. Code and trained checkpoints are available at https://github.com/Aaddy-1/hgq-jetformer.

item.title: Characterization of a hybrid superconducting RF cavity for use in axion searches
item.description: arXiv:2611.00087v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We report on the development of a hybrid superconducting radio-frequency (SRF) cavity for axion haloscopes. The Axion Dark Matter eXperiment (ADMX) Sidecar has been a program of ADMX for testing technologies with the potential for improving high frequency cavity haloscopes in the 4-6 GHz range. A replica of the Sidecar cavity, an aluminum clamshell microwave resonator loaded with a niobium tuning rod coated with Nb3Sn, was characterized in a dilution fridge through its critical temperature transitions down to 25 mK and through magnetic fields up to 6 T. The quality factor of five resonant modes of the cavity system were monitored throughout the process, including the TM010 mode used in axion searches. Distinct superconducting transitions were observed near the expected critical temperatures of Nb3Sn, pure niobium, and aluminum. The TM010 mode exhibited a factors of improvement in quality factor of 1.86 and 2.87 through the two niobium transitions, which implied the rod had a zero-field surface resistance of roughly 79% that of copper at cryogenic temperatures. Magnet tests showed a distinct superconducting transition for aluminum, and gradual degradation of quality factor expected for Nb3Sn in a mixed superconducting state. This hybrid resonator design has been integrated in the ADMX insert for performing an axion-like particle search.

item.title: The liquid-phase xenon purification system of the XENONnT dark matter experiment
item.description: arXiv:2611.00093v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The XENONnT dark matter experiment utilizes a dual-phase time projection chamber (TPC) housed in a cryostat filled with 8.5 t of ultra-pure liquid xenon. To achieve optimal sensitivity, free electrons generated by particle interactions are required to drift across the 1.5-meter detector under an electric field. Dissolved impurities, particularly oxygen (O$_2$), can attenuate the resulting charge signal due to electron attachment. XENONnT demands an O$_2$-equivalent concentration below 100 parts per trillion (ppt) to enable its dark matter sensitivity reach. A novel liquid-phase xenon purification system was developed that continuously circulates liquid xenon through custom-designed, packed-bed sorbent purifier units at a volumetric flow rate of $\sim$2 liters per minute (L/min) at a cryogenic temperature around 175 K. With a purification time constant of approximately 25 h, the system reached the required purity within five days. The purification strategy employs a two-step approach: For an initial cleanup, a purifier based on a copper catalyst on high-surface-area alumina support (Q5) removes impurities from the liquid xenon bulk with nearly 100% efficiency, ideal for initial detector filling or after long-term maintenance. However, the high $^{222}$Rn emanation rate of the Q5 catalyst leads to increased background in the detector. In a second step, a purifier with sintered pellets of non-evaporable getter alloy (St707) ensures sustained purity with negligible background impact. The St707-based purifier exhibits a 55% efficiency, sufficient for normal operation. Following system commissioning, XENONnT achieved an O$_2$-equivalent concentration in liquid xenon below 19 ppt during its first science run. With this exceptional purity, over 86% of generated electrons survive a full drift across the TPC.

item.title: SpikePID: Real-Time Neuromorphic Cluster Counting in Future Drift Chambers
item.description: arXiv:2611.00104v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cluster counting ($dN/dx$) measures discrete ionization occurrences along a charged particle track traversing a gaseous medium and is currently being proposed to serve particle identification (PID) in next-generation drift chambers, as it is expected to offer higher separation power than the traditional approach based on the ionization energy loss measurement ($dE/dx$), which has intrinsically larger statistical fluctuations. However, measuring $dN/dx$ in drift chambers proposed for future colliders requires high-resolution waveforms, which result in very large data rates. Running the reconstruction at the edge would drastically reduce the bandwidth required to transmit data off the detector. In this paper, we introduce SpikePID, a neuromorphic computing approach applying spiking neural networks (SNNs) to this task due to their inherently sparse computing and processing nature. We show that an SNN with only 529 parameters improves the kaon-pion separation power by 17% over the traditional derivative-based method and by 4% over an MLP that has $8.6\times$ more parameters. When synthesized to an FPGA, it uses an order of magnitude fewer resources than the MLP, and has an inference latency compatible with the constraints of future collider experiments, making the SNN an excellent algorithmic candidate for real-time data readout in future drift chambers.
item.dc:creator: Ho Fung Tsoi, Kam Wai Lai, Dylan Rankin

item.title: Highly polarized epithermal neutron beam using polarized 3He gas at J-PARC
item.description: arXiv:2611.00106v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We have realized a highly polarized epithermal neutron beam using an in-situ polarized 3He spin filter at the high-intensity pulsed neutron facility J-PARC. A neutron polarization exceeding 80% was achieved for epithermal neutrons with energies below 1 eV, including a polarization of 86.4 $\pm$ 0.5% for 0.75 eV neutrons, which corresponds to the resonance energy of the p-wave compound state in the 139La+n system. The spin filter consisted of a 20-cm-long, 3.2-atm 3He gas cell polarized on the beamline using a compact laser-optics system for spin-exchange optical pumping (SEOP). A 3He polarization of approximately 78% was stably maintained on the beamline for more than 100 hours. The polarized epithermal neutron beam developed in this work provides a powerful tool for studies of discrete symmetry violations, including measurements of enhanced parity violation in neutron absorption by medium-heavy nuclei such as 139La and searches for time-reversal symmetry violation in neutron-nucleus systems.

item.title: Characterization of Next Generation Power Over Fiber Systems under Cryogenic Conditions for Advanced Physics Instrumentation
item.description: arXiv:2611.00115v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The successful application of Power-over-Fiber (PoF) technology to power photon detection systems in DUNE prototypes operating under high-voltage and cryogenic conditions has laid the groundwork for the next generation of PoF systems operating in harsh environments. This paper presents the characterization of the main components of a new PoF system operating at 1470 and 1550 nm, including the measurement of the electrical-to-optical conversion efficiency of laser transmitters, the optical-to-electrical conversion efficiency of commercial optical power converters (OPCs), and the estimation of optical fiber attenuation under cryogenic conditions. In addition, a detailed characterization of the response of silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) to light leakage from optical fibers and OPCs is presented, using 808 nm as a reference to evaluate the reduction in the SiPM response at longer wavelengths. The results of this work provide a foundation for the development of next-generation PoF systems capable of powering electronics and electrical systems for future high-energy physics experiments. In addition, the electrical isolation, low-noise operation, and long-term reliability of PoF technology could motivate its application in other research fields requiring remote power delivery under cryogenic conditions, as well as in systems where infrared photons could affect their performance.
item.dc:creator: J. Rodr\'iguez Rondon, D. Leon Silverio, H. Wolf, D. A. Martinez Caicedo, W. Pellico

item.title: A Scalable Two-Stage Back-End Architecture for 400GbE Data Acquisition Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.00116v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A primary challenge in High Energy Physics (HEP) data acquisition is the aggregation of numerous low-speed (10 Gb/s) radiation-hard data links into high-speed back-end interfaces. While high-end FPGAs traditionally perform this task, transceiver density and speed in modern devices can limit cost-effective scaling. This study proposes a two-stage architecture that utilizes mid-range FPGAs for decoding and Ethernet conversion, followed by a Microchip META-DX2+ Ethernet PHY that aggregates these streams into a 400 GbE interface. This study evaluates the design's performance, validating it as a scalable and cost-effective architecture for next-generation HEP data acquisition systems.
item.dc:creator: Alberto Perro, Paolo Durante, Tommaso Colombo

item.title: Localized anomaly detection with a calorimeter normalizing flow
item.description: arXiv:2611.00234v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Normalizing flows trained as fast calorimeter simulators also give the likelihood of each shower, which can serve as an anomaly score. Because this likelihood sums over every voxel, a signal confined to a few voxels can be lost in the fluctuations of the rest of the shower. For example, in a public benchmark dataset in which a long-lived neutral particle decays to two photons, the CaloFlow likelihood used in previous work selects less than 5% of the signal at a background efficiency of $10^{-3}$ when the particle has the largest simulated mass and decays at or just behind the front face of the calorimeter. In this work, we define a regional anomaly score by summing the squared latent coordinates of the same flow within small detector regions around the point where the particle enters the calorimeter, with the threshold set using background showers alone. At the same background efficiency, this regional anomaly score selects more than 95% of the signal. The per-coordinate likelihood terms, summed over the same regions, perform equally well, but the squared latent coordinates have a known distribution for background showers and clearly illustrate when a shower departs from it. Therefore, normalizing flows may be sensitive to new physics, even if the global likelihood is not.
item.dc:creator: Raunav Mendiratta, Jason Weitz, Javier Duarte

item.title: Low Frequency Noise Identification for the SuperCDMS Experiment using Convolutional Neural Networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.00248v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The SuperCDMS experiment uses semiconductor crystal detectors operated at cryogenic temperatures to search for low-mass dark matter. Vibrations observed during the SuperCDMS Soudan experiment generated broadband low-frequency noise (LFN), which due to its similarity in the pulse shape to the low-energy signal events is difficult to remove. In the final low ionization threshold analysis, CDMSlite Run 3, the strong event selection criterion applied to remove LFN events also significantly reduced the ability to identify signal events in the low energy region, thus reducing the sensitivity of the experiment to low-mass dark matter. Therefore, an LFN rejection criterion using machine learning (ML) aimed to improve the signal efficiency while maintaining the signal purity has now been developed. This paper presents a new method using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), its application to the CDMSlite Run 3 dataset, and its impact on dark matter sensitivities, with further investigation through case studies.

item.title: Sealed, Lightweight gRPC-Based Muon Telescopes for Muography Applications
item.description: arXiv:2611.00369v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Portable muon detection systems are increasingly in demand for muography applications in environments requiring flexible installation and transportability. We present the ongoing development and implementation of portable muon tracking systems based on glass Resistive Plate Chambers (gRPCs). The work addresses the fabrication and assembly of compact, position-sensitive RPC detectors, along with their performance when operated with a standard gas mixture and coupled to external front-end electronics and a scalable multi-channel data-acquisition system. The system design prioritizes modular construction, mechanical robustness, operational safety, autonomous functionality, and cost-effectiveness. Measurements with atmospheric muons demonstrated stable detector performance and reliable tracking capability, confirming the suitability of this architecture for muographic measurements. We conclude with an outlook on further developments of the detection system.

item.title: Optical Acceptance Testing of Serenity-S1 Boards for the CMS HGCAL Phase-2 Backend Electronics
item.description: arXiv:2611.00418v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The CMS Phase-2 upgrade includes a new high-granularity calorimeter. The calorimeter electronics will include around 300 Serenity-S1 FPGA boards that use Samtec FireFly electro-optical modules with a link speed of up to 25 Gbps. General production tests performed by the central Serenity group only validate the high-speed links via copper loopback cables. We present an optical acceptance test framework specifically designed for the calorimeter, providing comprehensive link and slow-control validation of installed FireFly modules under realistic operating conditions. This test combines loopback and board-to-board testing, extended bit error ratio measurements, and continuous module health monitoring within an automated workflow, delivering structured diagnostics and ensuring reliable large-scale system deployment.

item.title: Optimal Fan-Out and Break-Even Routing Loss in Waveguide-Integrated Ge-on-Si SPAD Arrays
item.description: arXiv:2611.01111v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Splitting a waveguide mode over several Ge-on-Si single-photon avalanche diodes (SPADs) relieves dead-time saturation but multiplies dark counts. We quantify this trade-off with the asymptotic count-based information rate, which prices dark counts and dead time in one unit and is attained by an optimally weighted moment estimator. For a non-paralyzable pixel, the information per pre-dead-time signal event peaks at a signal rate $y^*=\sqrt{D(D+1/\tau)}$ with exact efficiency $(\sqrt{1+D\tau}-\sqrt{D\tau})^2$, which sets the optimal fan-out and a critical flux above which equal splitting is optimal. We then compare four routing architectures on 64 simulated 16-pixel arrays: an equal passive tree, static trees (uncalibrated, and an idealized calibration-informed benchmark), an ideal programmable tree, and a thermo-optic Mach-Zehnder interferometer (MZI) tree with 1.32 dB excess loss. Ideal programmability gains up to 15.9 dB over equal splitting at low flux. At one known flux, however, the calibrated static splitter beats the MZI tree by 0.14-2.7 dB, and the penalty tends to twice the excess loss when dark counts dominate. In ensemble-median worst-case regret, the MZI tree breaks even only for flux windows wider than 2.55 decades, and not within six decades above about 3.4 dB excess loss. Event-level Monte Carlo simulations reproduce the count statistics and the predicted estimator variances within bootstrap confidence intervals. Sensitivity analyses cover dark-count level, heterogeneity, detector model and random seed. All results are simulations with representative literature parameters.

item.title: Muography Simulations for Carbon Capture and Storage Monitoring
item.description: arXiv:2611.01668v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Muography can monitor CO2 storage through reservoir density changes, but site-scale simulations are costly: reservoirs can be deep and borehole detectors are small. We address both with two approaches. First, a two-stage workflow splits the kilometer-scale simulation: a fast code transports muons through the overburden, and a general-purpose Monte Carlo code through the reservoir and detectors. Second, a geometric filter at the source keeps only muons whose direction and position let them reach the detectors, within a margin for multiple scattering, and a range cut removes those with too little energy. Both are available in the UCMuon simulation suite for muon generation, filtering and transport. At a deep (800-1000 m) and a shallow (65 m) CO2 storage site, each approach reduces the computing time about 700-fold, and the filtered simulation gives the same hit rate as a full one, as long as the margin exceeds the muons' sideways scattering drift.
item.dc:creator: Hamid Basiri, Andrea Giammanco, Jun Matsushima, Mohammed Y. Ali, Eduardo Cortina Gil, Ahmed Eleslambouly, Hiroyuki K. M. Tanaka

item.title: Self-driven beta-radiation detection through a graphene/water/silicon heterostructure
item.description: arXiv:2611.01681v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large-volume neutrino observatories, exemplified by IceCube, exploit Cherenkov light generated by neutrino-induced charged particles in Antarctic ice, highlighting the potential of water-based media for high-energy particle detection. In $\beta$-decay, a neutron converts into a proton via the weak interaction, emitting an electron and an electron antineutrino. The electron constitutes the beta radiation detected in this work, while the accompanying antineutrino motivates future extensions toward neutrino detection. Here we demonstrate a complementary electrical transduction strategy using a graphene/water/silicon heterostructure that generates reversible current transients under beta irradiation at zero applied bias. Energetic electrons deposit energy in silicon, producing nonequilibrium carriers that perturb the semiconductor surface potential and electric displacement across the adjacent aqueous interface. The resulting redistribution of interfacial water polarization drives a transient compensation current, whereas carrier relaxation restores the initial polarization state and generates an opposite-polarity recovery signal. The complete irradiation-detector-electrometer system exhibits exponential rise and recovery time constants of approximately 1.0 and 3.6 ms, respectively. The response is strongly regulated by water-layer thickness and ionic composition, and the 17 beam pulses of a programmed 1 s sequence at 17 Hz are resolved individually. Integration with Ce:YAG further introduces a scintillation-mediated excitation pathway. These findings establish interfacial water polarization as a tunable, zero-bias electrical transduction mechanism for time-resolved beta-radiation monitoring and motivate future investigations of higher-energy charged particles and secondary particles relevant to neutrino detection.
item.dc:creator: Tengfei Wu, Kangchen Xiong, Minhui Yang, Xin Chen, Shisheng Lin

item.title: Cryogenic Optoelectronic Characterization of InGaAsP LEDs for Low-Energy Detector Calibration
item.description: arXiv:2611.01776v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We measured the emission spectra and current-voltage (IV) characteristics of commercial InGaAsP LEDs in a cryostat over a temperature range from 7 K to 300 K. At a constant operating current of 3.3 mA, the peak emission wavelength of the 1200 nm (1650 nm) LED decreased from 1202.3 +/- 0.5 nm (1665.5 +/- 0.6 nm) at 300 K to 1143.1 +/- 0.3 nm (1539.5 +/- 2.2 nm) at 7 K, demonstrating a strong temperature dependence. The cut-in voltage increased systematically with decreasing temperature, in agreement with conventional diode theory. To assess junction self-heating effects, we conducted pulsed IV measurements at different duty cycles. The extracted apparent series resistance showed a clear duty-cycle dependence, whereas the cut-in voltage remained unchanged within experimental uncertainty, indicating that self-heating primarily influenced the IV slope rather than the cut-in voltage. These results quantitatively characterize the thermal behavior of both the spectral peak and key electrical parameters, supporting the application of InGaAsP LEDs as cryogenic calibration light sources.
item.dc:creator: Muad Ghaith, Wolfgang Rau, Philippe Di Stefano, Matthew Peterson-Galema, Eleanor Fascione, Richard Germond, Ryan Underwood

item.title: Cryogenic performance of Silicon Photo-Multipliers at LN$_2$ temperature and at 3 K in the RES-NOVA cryostat
item.description: arXiv:2611.01789v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Silicon Photo-Multipliers (SiPMs) are semiconductor-based photodetectors that offer performance comparable to that of traditional Photo-Multiplier Tubes (PMTs), while providing several advantages, including low operating voltage, immunity to magnetic fields, compact size, and mechanical robustness. These features have led to their widespread adoption in scintillator-based detectors for both fundamental and applied physics. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in the detection of scintillation light at cryogenic temperatures in low-temperature experiments based on bolometric detectors, such as RES-NOVA and CUPID, as well as in emerging quantum applications. In the RES-NOVA experiment, radiopure PbWO$_4$ crystals are used to detect supernova neutrinos. The scintillation of PbWO$_4$ can only be evaluated at cryogenic temperatures, as the scintillation light yield is negligible at room temperature. We present measurements of the performance at cryogenic temperatures of Hamamatsu S13360-1350CS SiPMs in terms of breakdown voltage and gain, at 77~K (in a liquid nitrogen bath) and at 3~K. The cooling down to 3~K has been carried out using a Proteox LX cryostat from Oxford Instruments.

item.title: Track reconstruction with ACTAR TPC: a transfer-reaction use case
item.description: arXiv:2611.02836v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A unified framework for track reconstruction in the ACTAR Time Projection Chamber (ACTAR TPC) is presented, designed to address the specific challenges of direct-reaction and resonance-elastic scattering experiments involving exotic nuclei. The actroot software package enables efficient semi-online analysis by integrating a continuity-based clustering algorithm followed by a modular filtering procedure to reduce noise, delta-electron contamination, and track fragmentation. The software was benchmarked with experimental data taken with a secondary 20O beam delivered by the LISE3 spectrometer at GANIL. The algorithm achieves reconstruction efficiencies exceeding 90% across various event topologies. The system provides accurate particle identification and reaction-point determination, facilitating the extraction of key physical observables. These results demonstrate the framework's suitability for its application to direct reaction experiments in cubic active-target TPCs without magnetic fields.
item.dc:creator: M. Lozano-Gonz\'alez, J. Lois-Fuentes, T. Roger, I. Blanco-Calvi\~no, B. Fern\'andez-Dom\'inguez

item.title: A combined segmented anode gas ionization chamber and time-of-flight detector for heavy ion elastic recoil detection analysis
item.description: arXiv:2611.03147v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A dedicated detector system for heavy ion elastic recoil detection analysis at the Tandem Laboratory of Uppsala University is presented. Benefits of combining a time-of-flight measurement with a segmented anode gas ionization chamber are demonstrated. The capability of ion species identification is improved with the present system, compared to that obtained when using a single solid state silicon detector for the full ion energy signal. The system enables separation of light elements, up to Neon, based on atomic number while signals from heavy elements such as molybdenum and tungsten are separated based on mass, to a sample depth on the order of one micrometer. The performance of the system is discussed and a selection of material analysis applications is given. Plasma-facing materials from fusion experiments, in particular metal mirrors, are used as a main example for the discussion. Marker experiments using nitrogen-15 or oxygen-18 are specific cases for which the described improved species separation and sensitivity are required. Resilience to radiation damage and significantly improved energy resolution for heavy elements at low energies are additional benefits of the gas ionization chamber over a solid state detector based system.

item.title: Fast Self-Triggering and Segment-Fitting of Cosmic Muons with a small-Diameter Monitored Drift Tube Detector
item.description: arXiv:2611.03369v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a fast self-triggering and segment-fitting algorithm that identifies cosmic muons and reconstructs their directions using a small-diameter Monitored Drift Tube (sMDT) chamber without an external trigger detector. The muon arrival time is determined using a Legendre-based algorithm combined with coarse- and fine-grid searches. We implement the algorithm in FPGA firmware on an ATLAS MDT miniDAQ board and evaluate its efficiency, resolution, and latency. The results demonstrate standalone sMDT triggering and trigger-level reconstruction of muon directions, providing a solution for chamber commissioning and potentially MDT-based triggers for charged massive stable particle searches at the High Luminosity-LHC.
item.dc:creator: Shuzhe Li, Yuxiang Guo, Jiajin Ge, Chihao Li, Bing Zhou, Junjie Zhu

item.title: Detecting Muons with a Siemens Biograph Vision Quadra
item.description: arXiv:2611.01845v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Atmospheric muons are routinely detected with a variety of instruments, from cloud chambers to scintillation detectors. In this study, we demonstrate that atmospheric muons can also be detected with a clinical long axial field-of-view positron emission tomograph (PET). We performed a blank scan without any radioactive source, using a prototype feature that records all single crystal interactions. The energy a muon deposits in the PET crystals far exceeds the upper limit of the recorded energy range, which means muons cannot be identified through energy discrimination. Instead, we used the scanner's time-of-flight capabilities to select crossing events, i.e. pairs of high-energy single crystal events across the PET gantry whose spatial and temporal separation is consistent with a downward-going ultrarelativistic particle. Random pairings, however, cannot be rejected on an event-by-event basis. We therefore established the muon origin of the crossing events through their characteristic angular distribution. In order to account for geometry and event selection bias, we compare the measured crossing events to a Monte Carlo simulation of muons following the expected angular distribution. This confirms that the measured crossing events in the PET scanner are consistent with atmospheric muons.
item.dc:creator: Lorenzo Mercolli, William M. Steinberger

item.title: Imaging the Current Distribution in Superconducting Transition-Edge Sensors with Scanning SQUID Microscopy
item.description: arXiv:2611.02352v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Transition-edge sensors (TESs) exploit the resistive transition of a superconductor to detect minute changes in temperature. While significant progress has been made in understanding the temperature- and current-dependent resistive transition in these devices, important aspects of TES behavior under bias remain unresolved. In particular, existing TES models largely neglect spatial variations in the superconducting state and current distribution arising from device geometry and proximity effects associated with the superconducting leads and normal metal features. Using scanning superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID) microscopy (SSM), we directly image local superconducting properties and transport current in two molybdenum-gold (MoAu) X-ray TES designs. We measure the local diamagnetic response to identify superconducting regions in devices voltage-biased within the transition and the Oersted field generated by the transport current to reconstruct the corresponding current distribution. We observe bias-dependent reconfigurations of the current distribution that track current-induced changes in superconducting regions, highlighting the importance of mesoscale spatial variations for TES device physics, operation, and design.
item.dc:creator: Samantha Walker, Austin Kaczmarek, Douglas A. Bennett, Jason E. Austermann, W. Bertrand Doriese, Shannon M. Duff, Johannes Hubmayr, Kelsey M. Morgan, Daniel R. Schmidt, Daniel S. Swetz, Joel N. Ullom, Joel Weber, Michael D. Niemack, Katja C. Nowack

item.title: Dual-Band Mid-Infrared Imaging for Measurement of Fuel Concentration and Temperature in a Supersonic Cavity
item.description: arXiv:2611.03341v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A dual-band mid-infrared absorption imaging method is demonstrated for spatially resolved measurement of ethylene concentration and temperature in a Mach-2 cavity flow. The method used narrowband filters selected to exploit the differing in-band temperature sensitivities of ethylene absorption, together with a broadband infrared source and high-frame-rate mid-wave infrared camera. Temperature-dependent, filter-weighted absorption cross-sections were used to measure two-dimensional ethylene number density and temperature fields. Measurements were obtained for cavity, curtain, and discrete fuel-injection configurations, including cases with the leading edge of a quasi-steady shock near the cavity. Cavity equivalence ratio measurements agreed well with independent extractive measurements and reproduced trends previously observed using hyperspectral imaging. A complementary single-band implementation using a temperature-independent filter provided instantaneous ethylene concentration fields at 100 Hz and revealed intermittent reductions in cavity equivalence ratio associated with plume deflection by the shock train leading edge. The dual-band approach provides quantitative full-field measurements with substantially simpler spectral instrumentation than hyperspectral imaging while retaining flexibility for time-resolved flow measurements.
item.dc:creator: Loren C. Hahn, Erik L. Braun, Brendan J. McGann, Katherine C. Opacich, Timothy M. Ombrello

item.title: Ton-scale Xenon Gas TPC for $0\nu\beta\beta$ Search at Atmospheric Pressure
item.description: arXiv:2609.07378v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We explore aspects of an unorthodox ton-scale xenon gas time projection chamber detector operated at normal temperature and pressure (NTP), designed for $0\nu\beta\beta$ discovery at $\sim10^{27}$ year sensitivity. At fixed active mass, a greater transparency to $\gamma$-ray backgrounds and better track clarity exists at NTP relative to higher density. Operation at NTP also alleviates difficulties with pressure containment and significantly reduces HV requirements. With metre-scale electron tracks at a few MeV, event topology can be used to efficiently reject the copious $\gamma$-ray backgrounds by factors ranging from 550--1200, largely compensating for the greater surface area of the detector. Event topology is captured from anode plane signals combined with sensing the secondary ion component arriving at the cathode plane. A molecular gas admixture limits diffusion of the secondary electron tracks to less than one cm rms and provides stable proportional avalanche gain for measurement of energy. An energy resolution $\delta$E/E $\leq$ 1\% FWHM seems possible. A 100 kg scale demonstrator for this detector technology could lead directly to a ton-scale search.
item.dc:creator: Y. Mei, K. Mistry, D. R. Nygren

item.title: Characterization of immersed SiPM arrays in liquid scintillator between room temperature and $-30\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$
item.description: arXiv:2609.25534v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Liquid scintillator detectors instrumented with distributed silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) arrays can be used in compact, topology-sensitive, and low-background experiments, but the temperature dependence of SiPMs immersed directly in the scintillation medium has not been widely characterized. We report the operation of a 125-liter linear-alkylbenzene-based liquid scintillator detector read out by 125 SiPM channels immersed in the active volume, over the range from room temperature to $-30\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The detector response was measured with cosmic-ray muons, including stopping muons followed by their Michel-electron decay. Cooling from $+15\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to $-30\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ reduced the SiPM dark-count rate by a factor of 13.5, increased the single-photoelectron response by 49.1%, and increased the cosmic-ray muon light yield by 16.7%. The improved photoelectron separation and baseline stability at low temperature enabled a selection of stopping-muon events, from which the effective muon lifetime was measured to be $1959\pm132\,\mathrm{ns}$, consistent with the value expected for a hydrocarbon scintillator once $\mu^{-}$ capture on carbon is taken into account.
item.dc:creator: M. S. Kwak, J. S. Chung, C. Ha, T. Z. Huang, J. Kim, S. A. Kim, H. Kimku, B. C. Koh, H. S. Lee, S. Lee, Y. J. Lee, J. Seo

item.title: Feed-forward active magnetic shielding
item.description: arXiv:2406.14234v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Measurement of small magnetic fields requires shielding. For example, magnetoencephalography (MEG) measures small fields arising within the brain, in the presence of environmental fields several orders of magnitude larger. A common solution is passive shielding, but its cost, bulk and limited effectiveness motivate the alternative approach of active shielding, which comes in two flavours: feed-back and feed-forward. In feed-back shielding (the most common design), coils are driven from sensors that measure the corrected field. In feed-forward shielding (less common), coils are driven from sensors that measure the uncorrected field. The latter has the potential of providing better performance, but its implementation is hobbled by an inevitable coupling between coils and reference sensors. This paper describes an approach that employs a data-driven ``decoupling matrix" to suppress the coupling, enabling greater flexibility to achieve effective shielding across a wide frequency range. The method is evaluated by simulation, first using a simplified "flat world" in which the principle is clearly visualised, and then based on the more realistic geometry of a standard MEG system. Performance appears to be limited only by spatial sampling and numerical resolution. The method, which is data-driven and does not require geometric calculations, tight-tolerance fabrication, or manual calibration, is complementary with standard feed-back shielding methods. Active shielding is of particular interest in the context of a new generation of optically-pumped magnetometers (OPM), as the lower cost and reduced constraints of these new systems relative to SQUID-based systems provide an incentive to likewise reduce the cost and constraints of shielding.
item.dc:creator: Alain de Cheveign\'e
